title: We Are Running Out of Sand and That Actually Matters
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the global sand crisis: sand is a finite, non-renewable resource being mined and shuffled worldwide faster than natural erosion replenishes it. They cover what sand is and how engineers classify it (river, ocean, and desert sand), its major uses (concrete, glass, asphalt, fracking, cosmetics), beach nourishment and its ecological costs, artificial islands in Dubai, Singapore, Indonesia and Morocco, dam and river sand mining (including the San Jacinto River and Hurricane Harvey), illegal sand mafias and violence, and possible alternatives like artificial sand and reduced concrete use. The episode closes with tour and live show promotions and a listener mail about the Portland, Maine show.

segments.title: Sand is finite and being shuffled around the world
segments.summary: The hosts say the world's sand is finite and rapidly depleting, with sand moved from poorer to wealthier areas and from rural to urban areas. They cite roughly 15 billion tons used for construction and about 40 billion tons mined yearly, and a UNEP report saying crushed rock, sand and gravel are the largest volume of extracted solid material. They note sand is effectively non-renewable.

segments.title: What sand is and how it forms
segments.summary: Sand forms from erosion by water, wind, ice and glaciers, and from volcanic lava, rain acid weathering, geological rock, and biological sources such as shell creatures and parrotfish that produce white sand. Sand is mostly quartz but can be gypsum, limestone, or lava.

segments.title: Sand definitions and types: river, ocean, desert
segments.summary: Engineers classify sand by size, not composition. The ASTM defines sand as particles between 75 microns and 4.75 millimeters. The hosts explain that river sand is irregular and best for construction, ocean sand is smooth, and desert sand is too round and uniform to be useful for building.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break before discussing how sand is used; hosts joke about candlesticks and malt liquor commercials.

segments.title: Uses of sand: glass, concrete, fracking, plastic
segments.summary: Sand is used for glass, silicon microchips, plastic, cosmetics, cleaners and grit, and fracking. Concrete is by far the largest use. Estimates given: about 200 tons per typical house, 3,000 tons for a school, 12 million tons for a nuclear plant, and roughly 30,000 tons per kilometer of interstate highway. Sand is locked into construction, so it stops circulating.

segments.title: Beach nourishment and its ecological impact
segments.summary: Beach nourishment or replenishment pumps or dredges sand onto eroding beaches. The hosts say it is preferable to sea walls, which block natural replenishment down-coast, but it kills organisms in the sand and disrupts the food web. Best practices include smaller incremental projects, timing around seabirds, and matching sand composition.

segments.title: Artificial islands, managed retreat, and sand dredging
segments.summary: Artificial islands are built with sand, and in Indonesia about 24 islands reportedly vanished from sand mining. Singapore has grown by about 20 percent through sand fill. Managed retreat, building far back from the beach, is discussed as an alternative. Dredging methods range from large suction dredges to manual digging.

segments.title: Illegal sand mining, sand mafias and violence
segments.summary: Much beach sand is illegally mined, around half in Morocco per the hosts, and the sand trade involves bribery and murder. Sand sells for about 10 to 20 dollars a ton, but its price has risen about sevenfold since the 1970s. In India the sand mafia has killed hundreds of people. Morocco's beaches have become rocky. Wired's 2015 article on the deadly global war for sand is cited.

segments.title: River and dam sand mining, flooding, and worker exploitation
segments.summary: The largest sand mine is Po Yang Lake near Shanghai. Mining along the San Jacinto River is thought to have worsened flooding in Hurricane Harvey in Houston. Dams trap sand from reaching river mouths. Divers in the ocean sand trade are poorly paid and face danger.

segments.title: Solutions: reduce concrete demand and artificial sand
segments.summary: The hosts compare the sand trade to the cocaine trade and suggest reducing demand. Alternatives include other building materials and crushed glass. Artificial sand made by grinding rock is currently too expensive but may become viable as real sand gets scarcer.

segments.title: Ventriloquist tangent and closing sand thoughts
segments.summary: A brief joking tangent about ventriloquists and a request to put sand conservation on listeners' radar at the beach.
